chapter.name: Nuclei
chapter.blurb: The chapter describes the atomic nucleus: its constituent protons and neutrons, its size and its enormous, constant density. It uses Einstein's mass-energy relation to define the mass defect and binding energy of a nucleus, reads the curve of binding energy per nucleon, and summarises the properties of the nuclear force. It closes with a brief qualitative account of radioactivity and with nuclear energy from fission and fusion, including energy generation in stars and controlled thermonuclear fusion.

scope_in.item: Define the atomic mass unit as 1/12th of the mass of a carbon-12 atom, and compute the atomic mass of an element as the abundance-weighted average of its isotope masses (chlorine example)

Describe the composition of the nucleus: protons and neutrons (nucleons), no electrons inside the nucleus, nuclear charge +Ze, the discovery of the neutron by Chadwick, the free neutron being unstable; use Z, N and A = Z + N and nuclide notation to count protons and neutrons
Identify and construct isotopes (same Z), isobars (same A) and isotones (same N), and explain why isotopes are chemically identical

Explain how nuclear size is inferred from alpha-particle scattering (distance of closest approach, deviation from Rutherford's calculation) and measured by electron scattering; use R = R0 A^(1/3) with R0 = 1.2 fm to find radii, ratios of radii and mass numbers (Exercise 13.4)

Show that nuclear volume is proportional to A and nuclear density is independent of A, compute the density of nuclear matter (about 2.3 x 10^17 kg/m^3), and compare it with ordinary matter and neutron stars (Example 13.1, Exercise 13.10)
Use E = mc^2 to find the energy equivalent of a mass and of one atomic mass unit (1 u = 931.5 MeV/c^2) (Examples 13.2, 13.3)

Calculate the mass defect [Z m_p + (A - Z) m_n] - M, the total binding energy E_b = Delta M c^2 and the binding energy per nucleon E_b/A from given masses, and state their physical meaning (Exercises 13.1-13.3)

State the main features of the curve of binding energy per nucleon against mass number (nearly constant for 30 < A < 170, maximum about 8.75 MeV at A = 56, 7.6 MeV at A = 238, lower for A < 30 and A > 170) and the conclusions drawn from it, including saturation and energy release in fission and fusion

State the properties of the nuclear force: much stronger than Coulomb and gravitational forces, short range and saturation, potential energy minimum at about 0.8 fm (attractive beyond, repulsive within), charge independence, no simple mathematical form
Describe radioactivity qualitatively: Becquerel's discovery, decay of an unstable nucleus, and what is emitted in alpha-, beta- and gamma-decay

Explain why nuclear transformations towards greater binding energy release energy, compare nuclear (MeV) with chemical (eV) energies, and use Q = (sum of initial masses - sum of final masses) c^2 to decide whether a reaction is exothermic or endothermic (Exercises 13.5, 13.6)

Describe neutron-induced fission of uranium-235, balance fission equations by proton and nucleon number, estimate the energy released from binding energies per nucleon (about 200 MeV), say how the energy appears, and compute energy from a given mass of fissile material (Exercise 13.7)
Explain in what sense nuclear reaction equations are balanced and how mass is converted to energy in nuclear and in chemical reactions (Example 13.4)

concepts.name: Atomic masses and the composition of the nucleus
concepts.description: The atomic mass unit, isotopes and the weighted-average atomic mass, the proton and the neutron, and the numbers Z, N and A that define isotopes, isobars and isotones.
concepts.idea: A nucleus is made of Z protons and N neutrons, A = Z + N nucleons in all, and atoms of one element can differ in mass because their nuclei hold different numbers of neutrons.
concepts.rule: Atomic masses are expressed in atomic mass units: 1 u is 1/12th of the mass of a carbon-12 atom, about 1.66 x 10^-27 kg. Atomic masses are measured with a mass spectrometer. Atoms of the same element that differ in mass are isotopes; practically every element is a mixture of isotopes and its atomic mass is the weighted average of their masses according to their relative abundances. Hydrogen has three isotopes: ordinary hydrogen, whose nucleus is the proton, deuterium and tritium (unstable, made artificially). The nucleus contains no electrons; all Z electrons lie outside it, so the nuclear charge is +Ze and the number of protons is exactly Z. The masses of the hydrogen, deuterium and tritium nuclei are as 1 : 2 : 3, which points to neutral matter in the nucleus; Chadwick (1932) identified it as the neutron, a neutral particle of mass very nearly that of the proton, from the neutral radiation emitted when beryllium is bombarded with alpha-particles. A free neutron is unstable but it is stable inside the nucleus. Z = atomic number = number of protons; N = neutron number; A = Z + N = mass number = number of nucleons. A nuclide is written with its chemical symbol, A and Z. Isotopes have the same Z and different N; isobars have the same A; isotones have the same N and different Z.
concepts.example: Carbon-13 (Z = 6) has 13 nucleons: 6 protons and N = 13 - 6 = 7 neutrons.

questions.q: Trace the chain of reasoning by which the neutron was established as a constituent of the nucleus: state what Chadwick observed, why that observation was a puzzle, and how he resolved it.
questions.a: Observation: when beryllium nuclei were bombarded with alpha-particles a neutral radiation was emitted, which could knock protons out of light nuclei such as helium, carbon and nitrogen. Puzzle: the only neutral radiation known then was photons, but conservation of energy and momentum showed that photons would need an energy much higher than is available from bombarding beryllium with alpha-particles. Resolution: Chadwick assumed the radiation consists of a new neutral particle, the neutron, and from conservation of energy and momentum found its mass to be very nearly the same as the mass of the proton.
s: Observation - neutral radiation from beryllium bombarded with alpha-particles, able to knock protons out of light nuclei
Puzzle - photons would need far more energy than is available (energy and momentum conservation)
Resolution - a new neutral particle, the neutron, of mass very nearly that of the proton

s: Judgement - not an error; chlorine is a mixture of isotopes each of nearly integral mass

concepts.name: Size of the nucleus and nuclear density
concepts.description: How nuclear sizes are found from scattering experiments, the relation R = R0 A^(1/3), and the constant, enormous density of nuclear matter.
concepts.idea: The volume of a nucleus grows in proportion to the number of nucleons in it, so every nucleus has practically the same, enormous, density - like drops of one liquid.
concepts.rule: The radius of a nucleus is smaller than that of an atom by a factor of about 10^4, so its volume is about 10^-12 of the atom's, while it holds more than 99.9 per cent of the mass. In the Geiger-Marsden experiment an alpha-particle of 5.5 MeV approaches a gold nucleus to about 4.0 x 10^-14 m and the scattering is explained by coulomb repulsion alone, so the nucleus is smaller than this. With more energetic alpha-particles the scattering eventually deviates from Rutherford's calculation because the short-range nuclear force acts; the distance at which deviations set in gives the nuclear size. Scattering of fast electrons has given accurate sizes. A nucleus of mass number A has radius R = R0 A^(1/3) with R0 = 1.2 x 10^-15 m = 1.2 fm (1 fm = 10^-15 m). The volume, proportional to R^3, is proportional to A, so the density of nuclear matter is independent of A: about 2.3 x 10^17 kg/m^3, very large compared with water (10^3 kg/m^3) because ordinary matter is mostly empty space. Matter in neutron stars has a comparable density.

questions.a: Fire alpha-particles at a thin foil of the element and record how they are scattered, repeating the experiment with alpha-particles of higher and higher kinetic energy so that the distance of closest approach to the nucleus becomes smaller and smaller. As long as the two agree, the nucleus must be smaller than the distance of closest approach. At some energy the scattering begins to deviate because the short-range nuclear force comes into play; the distance of closest approach at which the deviations set in gives the size of the nucleus.
s: Vary - the kinetic energy of the alpha-particles, so that the distance of closest approach decreases
Compare - the observed scattering with Rutherford's pure coulomb-repulsion calculation
Read - the distance at which deviations set in (nuclear force acting) gives the nuclear size

concepts.name: Mass-energy, mass defect and nuclear binding energy
concepts.description: Einstein's mass-energy relation, the energy equivalent of the atomic mass unit, the mass defect of a nucleus, and its binding energy in total and per nucleon.
concepts.idea: A nucleus weighs less than the protons and neutrons it is made of; the missing mass, multiplied by c^2, is the energy that holds it together.
concepts.rule: Mass is another form of energy: E = m c^2, with c about 3 x 10^8 m/s; energy is conserved in a reaction provided the energy associated with mass is included. The energy equivalent of one atomic mass unit is 1 u = 931.5 MeV/c^2. The mass M of a nucleus is always less than the total mass of its constituents; the difference is the mass defect, Delta M = [Z m_p + (A - Z) m_n] - M. The binding energy is E_b = Delta M c^2: it is released when the nucleons are brought together to form the nucleus, and it is the total energy that would have to be supplied to separate the nucleus into its nucleons. The binding energy per nucleon is E_bn = E_b / A, the average energy per nucleon needed to separate the nucleus into its nucleons; it is the more useful measure of how tightly the nucleus is bound. When atomic masses are given, either subtract the Z electron masses to get the nuclear mass, or use the mass of the hydrogen atom in place of the proton mass so that the electron masses cancel.

concepts.name: The binding energy curve and the nuclear force
concepts.description: The main features of the plot of binding energy per nucleon against mass number, the conclusions drawn from it, and the properties of the nuclear force.
concepts.idea: The binding energy per nucleon is nearly the same for all middle-mass nuclei because each nucleon is bound only by its near neighbours - the nuclear force is strong but short-ranged.
concepts.rule: In the plot of binding energy per nucleon E_bn against mass number A: (i) E_bn is practically constant for nuclei of middle mass number (30 < A < 170); the curve has a maximum of about 8.75 MeV at A = 56 and a value of 7.6 MeV at A = 238; (ii) E_bn is lower for both light nuclei (A < 30) and heavy nuclei (A > 170). Conclusions: the force is attractive and strong enough to give a binding energy of a few MeV per nucleon; the constancy of E_bn follows from the short range of the nuclear force (a nucleon is influenced only by neighbours within range - the saturation property); a very heavy nucleus breaking into two middle-mass nuclei, or two very light nuclei joining into a heavier one, gives more tightly bound nucleons and releases energy. The nuclear force is much stronger than the Coulomb force (gravitation is weaker still); it falls rapidly to zero beyond a few femtometres; the potential energy of two nucleons is a minimum at about r0 = 0.8 fm, the force being attractive for larger separations and strongly repulsive for smaller ones; it is approximately the same between n-n, p-n and p-p (it does not depend on charge); it has no simple mathematical form.
concepts.example: A nucleus of mass number 150 with a binding energy per nucleon of 8.2 MeV has a total binding energy of 150 x 8.2 = 1230 MeV.

questions.a: Axes: mass number A along the horizontal axis and binding energy per nucleon (in MeV) along the vertical axis. Features: the curve rises steeply for light nuclei, is practically constant at about 8 MeV for 30 < A < 170 with a maximum of about 8.75 MeV at A = 56, and then falls slowly to about 7.6 MeV at A = 238; the binding energy per nucleon is lower for both light nuclei (A < 30) and heavy nuclei (A > 170). Energy regions: at the heavy end a very heavy nucleus can break into two middle-mass nuclei that are more tightly bound, releasing energy (fission); at the light end very light nuclei can join into a heavier, more tightly bound nucleus, releasing energy (fusion).
s: Axes - mass number A horizontal, binding energy per nucleon in MeV vertical
Features - nearly constant for 30 < A < 170, maximum about 8.75 MeV at A = 56, about 7.6 MeV at A = 238, lower at both ends
Energy regions - fission of very heavy nuclei and fusion of very light nuclei both move towards tighter binding

concepts.name: Radioactivity, nuclear energy and fission
concepts.description: The qualitative account of radioactive decay, why nuclear transformations release energy, the Q value of a nuclear reaction, and the fission of heavy nuclei.
concepts.idea: Energy is released whenever less tightly bound nuclei turn into more tightly bound ones, as when a heavy nucleus splits into two middle-mass fragments.
concepts.rule: Radioactivity (Becquerel, 1896) is a nuclear phenomenon in which an unstable nucleus undergoes a decay. Three types occur in nature: alpha-decay, in which a helium-4 nucleus is emitted; beta-decay, in which electrons or positrons (same mass as the electron, opposite charge) are emitted; gamma-decay, in which high-energy photons (hundreds of keV or more) are emitted. The greater the binding energy, the less the total mass of a bound system, so when nuclei with less total binding energy transform to nuclei with greater binding energy there is a net release of energy. The energy in nuclear reactions is of the order of MeV against electron volts in chemical reactions: for the same quantity of matter nuclear sources give about a million times more energy. Q = (sum of initial masses - sum of final masses) c^2 = final kinetic energy - initial kinetic energy; Q positive is exothermic, Q negative endothermic. In a nuclear reaction the number of protons and the number of neutrons are each conserved, and the energy released is the difference in total binding energy of the two sides. In fission a heavy nucleus such as uranium-235, bombarded with a neutron, breaks into two intermediate-mass fragments and a few neutrons, releasing energy of the order of 200 MeV per fission; the fragments are radioactive and emit beta particles in succession. The energy appears first as kinetic energy of the fragments and neutrons and finally as heat. Nuclear reactors use fission; an atom bomb is uncontrolled fission.
concepts.example: neutron + uranium-235 -> antimony-133 (Z = 51) + niobium-99 (Z = 41) + 4 neutrons: protons 92 = 51 + 41 and nucleons 236 = 133 + 99 + 4.

questions.q: Evaluate the general impression that 'mass-energy interconversion takes place only in nuclear reactions and never in chemical reactions'.
questions.a: Strictly, the impression is incorrect. The energy released or absorbed in a chemical reaction comes from the difference in chemical binding energies of the atoms and molecules on the two sides, and chemical binding energy also gives a negative contribution (a mass defect) to the mass. So mass is converted into energy in a chemical reaction too; the mass defects involved are almost a million times smaller than in a nuclear reaction, which is why they go unnoticed.
s: Judgement - incorrect; chemical binding energy also contributes a mass defect, so mass-energy interconversion occurs in chemical reactions as well

concepts.name: Nuclear fusion and energy generation in stars
concepts.description: Fusion of light nuclei, the coulomb barrier and thermonuclear fusion, the proton-proton cycle in the sun, and controlled thermonuclear fusion.
concepts.idea: Light nuclei release energy when they fuse, but they must first be energetic enough to get past their mutual coulomb repulsion - which is why fusion needs the temperatures found inside stars.
concepts.rule: When two light nuclei fuse into a larger nucleus energy is released, because the larger nucleus is more tightly bound. For fusion the nuclei must come within the short range of the attractive nuclear force, so they need enough energy to overcome the coulomb barrier, whose height depends on the charges and radii of the nuclei (about 400 keV for two protons, higher for higher charges). Setting (3/2) k T equal to 400 keV gives T of about 3 x 10^9 K. Fusion achieved by raising the temperature is thermonuclear fusion; it is the source of energy in stars. The sun's interior is at 1.5 x 10^7 K, so fusion there involves protons with energies much above the average. The sun burns the hydrogen in its core into helium by the proton-proton cycle, whose net effect is that four hydrogen atoms form one helium-4 atom with a release of 26.7 MeV. When the core hydrogen is depleted a star's core collapses and heats; at about 10^8 K helium fuses into carbon, but elements more massive than those near the peak of the binding energy curve cannot be produced by fusion. The sun, about 5 x 10^9 years old, has hydrogen for about another 5 billion years and will then become a red giant. Controlled fusion reactors aim at steady power by heating the fuel to about 10^8 K, where it is a plasma; the challenge is to confine the plasma, since no container can stand such a temperature.
concepts.example: Two deuterons (hydrogen-2 nuclei) can fuse to form a triton (hydrogen-3 nucleus) and a proton.

Calculate the height of the coulomb barrier for a head-on collision of two deuterons, in keV. In joules: 6.43 x 10^14 J

questions.q: Draw up an outline proposal for a power source on the earth that copies the way a star produces its energy. State the process it would use and its aim, the conditions the fuel must be brought to, and the main obstacle your design would have to overcome.
questions.a: Process and aim: use thermonuclear fusion of light nuclei, the process that powers stars, in a controlled way so as to generate steady power. Conditions: the nuclear fuel has to be heated to a temperature in the range of 10^8 K so that the nuclei have enough energy to overcome their coulomb repulsion; at this temperature the fuel is a plasma, a mixture of positive ions and electrons. Obstacle: the plasma has to be confined, and no material container can stand such a high temperature, so the design must provide a way of holding the plasma without letting it touch any wall. If this succeeds, such reactors could supply almost unlimited power.
s: Process and aim - controlled thermonuclear fusion of light nuclei to give steady power
Conditions - fuel heated to about 10^8 K, where it is a plasma of positive ions and electrons
Obstacle - confining the plasma, since no container can stand that temperature
